description: We're two students from Hsinchu High School. We absolutely love mapping and creating. One of us has created a walking route app, plus we both have experience coding web apps. For the Martian Map challenge, we would like to present NASA data in an intuitive and useful way for a Mars explorer. We would be happy to have a teammate who is passionate about any of the following: Mars Science, Geology, Data Visualisation, or Design. You can speak either English or Chinese.
summary:
SUIT ALARM at Three Forks, the walk's farthest stop. Backup oxygen: 1 hour. Walk home: 42 minutes. Getting inside: about 10. Do they make it? Yes, with 8 minutes to spare, because Red Route planned the walk around this moment.

Red Route is a web map that plans a Jezero Crater Marswalk for the bad day, so the crew always gets home. Every minute must pass three checks: home in time at normal pace; home in time at half speed, helping a hurt crewmate, reserve untouched; and never more than 50 minutes' walk from base, so the backup oxygen always lasts. It turns 10.6 million NASA HiRISE height points into a walking time for every 2 m of ground, layers data from five NASA missions, and gives every stop a "leave by" time.

In 1,000 simulated bad days (walks up to 20 % slower, a crewmate hurt at a random moment), a usual-rule plan needed its reserve 320 times; our rule at its limit, 111; our plan, 18. Against Perseverance's tilt sensor at 189 points, our slopes are off by 1.33° on average (a flat guess: 3.57°).

Limits: suit numbers are NASA's Moon numbers; rocks under 1.5 m are unmapped.
details:
Red Route: plan for the bad day

Most walks are planned for a good day. Red Route plans a Marswalk in Jezero Crater for the day something goes wrong. At every minute of the walk, the crew of two must still be able to walk home at half speed, one helping the other, with the 30 % reserve untouched and 2 h of airlock time already taken off. Add one science stop too many and the app says so: the plan fails by 57 minutes.

Why the plan has to carry the answer: a radio signal takes 3 to 22 minutes each way between Earth and Mars (NASA), so a question to Earth and its answer take 6 to 44 minutes. The turn-back call has to be made on Mars.

Picture: the planner as it opens. NASA's HiRISE map of Jezero Crater, the planned walk, and the three get-home checks with their breaking points. The walk and the clock are simulated.

Try it in 90 seconds

  1. Open the app and press "Walk the plan". The green zone is where the crew can still get home from.
  2. Press "Crewmate hurt here" at any moment. The app answers from that exact spot: MAKES IT or DOES NOT MAKE IT.
  3. Press "Storm warning now", then "Real storm". The solar storm of 20 May 2024 is replayed from Curiosity's readings.
  4. Open "Plan your EVA" and tick the third stop, Tenby. "Plan fits" turns to FAIL, 57 minutes over.

Picture: one stop too many. With the third stop, Tenby, ticked, "Plan fits" fails by 57 minutes.

What it does

  • It plans the walk: base camp, the Three Forks sample depot (10 sample tubes left by Perseverance), the layered rocks at Hawksbill Gap, and back. 2.35 km, never steeper than 14.8°, 2 h 53 min outside.
  • It checks every point three ways: home at normal pace (43 min to spare); home at half speed with a hurt crewmate (14 min to spare); never more than 50 min from base (the longest walk home is 42 min, the tightest check).
  • It gives every stop a leave-by time: T+2:11 at Three Forks, T+2:37 at Hawksbill Gap.
  • It shows how close each check is to failing: the walk still passes 32 %, 10 % and 15 % slower.
  • It tests the bad day: four drill buttons (crewmate hurt, suit alarm, storm warning, running late) and a "What if here?" click anywhere on the map. The storm drill can replay a real storm.
  • It goes with the crew: an Astronaut view that says one word (GO, HEAD HOME SOON or TURN BACK NOW), a one-page printed cuff card, and a 3D walk of the plan at true scale with the same numbers.

Picture: the Astronaut view at T+3:04 with the third stop ticked. It says TURN BACK NOW; in this frame the hurt-crewmate case is 15 minutes short (13 to 16 within that minute). A simulated walk, not a real suit.

Picture: the same app on a phone. Left: the walk playing, with the numbers and the four drill buttons under the map. Right: the storm drill replaying the real storm.

How it works

  1. We read 10.6 million height points from NASA's 1 m HiRISE elevation model and compute slope and rough ground on a 2 m grid of 2.66 million cells.
  2. Every cell gets a walking time: NASA's 2 km/h planning pace on flat ground, slower on slopes and rough ground, and no-go above 15° (our choice; NASA's suit requirement is 20°).
  3. One path search links the stops. A second one stores the walk-home time from every cell. That one layer drives every check, leave-by time and drill.
  4. The time budget is NASA's 8 h suit limit, minus a 30 % reserve (our choice), minus 2 h of airlock time (NASA's Artemis III EVA study). That leaves 3 h 36 min outside.
  5. Drag a stop or move a rule and the whole plan is worked out again in the browser in about a second.

What we checked, and what failed

  • We checked the slope map against Perseverance's tilt sensor, which never saw our map. At 189 waypoint records our map is off by 1.33° on average; a flat guess with no map is off by 3.57°. Limit: where the rover tilted more than 10°, our map reads about 1.4° low. That is the unsafe side.
  • We checked if our route follows the rover's. It does not: on the rover's climb it stays a median 173 m from its track. What holds: a straight line there crosses 154 m of ground steeper than 15°, the rover crossed 28 m, and our route none. Straight lines between our own stops would cross 58 m. Limit: "none" is a rule in the planner, not a test result.
  • We checked a slower crew. The walk still passes 32 %, 10 % and 15 % slower, check by check. Limit: a crew slower than about 0.51 m/s fails the bad-day check on this walk.
  • We checked if the rule pays off. Three plans on the same stops, in the same 1,000 simulated walks (each up to 20 % slower than planned, a crewmate hurt at a random moment). A plan made with the usual walk-back rule needed its reserve 320 times. A plan made with our rule, using all the time it allows: 111 times. Our own plan, which also keeps 14 minutes spare: 18 times. Then we replaced our assumed slowdown with NASA's Apollo records (travel time against plan on 8 moonwalks, 0.69 to 1.83 times the plan): 368, 256 and 224 times. Limit: the first two plans are our own constructions and the 0 to 20 % range is our assumption. The Apollo spread is harsher, and with it even our plan needs its reserve in about one walk in five; it is the Moon, mostly rover drives, and only 8 moonwalks. Our rule costs 29 minutes at the science stops. Nobody went past the suit limit in any run.
  • We checked a real solar storm. We replayed the storm of 20 May 2024 from the readings of Curiosity's radiation detector (NASA's public archive). The strongest reading began 37 minutes after our alarm. From the farthest point of the walk the crew needs 53 minutes to be inside, so it is still outside at the peak and takes about 240 microgray on the way (a quiet day: about 5). Limit: readings are 8 to 16 minutes long, so 37 could be 28 to 54; the rise is the storm arriving, so there is no earlier warning in this data; it was measured on the rover's deck in Gale Crater, not in a suit in Jezero. Our alarm line (1.5 times normal) is our own choice; the 25 % rule the RAD team published (Löwe et al. 2025, Space Weather), applied by us to the same readings, picks the same reading.
  • We checked the published storm-shelter advice. The same paper advises not going more than 30 minutes from shelter. Our walk fails it: from the farthest point the crew needs 53 minutes to be inside. We say so in the app, and an optional map layer draws the 30-minute line. Limit: it is a research result from past storms at Gale Crater, not a NASA flight rule, and our three checks do not use it.
  • We checked base camp as a landing site. It fails: the ground reaches 19.5° within 100 m. We say so in the app.
  • 90 automated tests re-check these numbers, the simulation with its Apollo case, the Apollo sums and the storm replay. The app's "How it works" has the same table.

Picture: the storm drill at the farthest point of the walk, replaying the solar storm of 20 May 2024 from the readings of NASA Curiosity's radiation detector. The crew needs 53 minutes to be inside; the strongest reading began 37 minutes after the alarm. A replay, not a forecast.

Picture: part of "What we checked, and what failed" in the app. Every claim sits next to its limit.

How it answers the challenge

  • A layered view of one walk, from five NASA missions: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Mars Global Surveyor, Mars 2020 Perseverance, Mars Odyssey and Curiosity, plus NASA's DONKI space-weather database and ESA's Mars Express.
  • More than three kinds of data: optical, topographic, thermal, atmospheric, radiation, space weather and 64 rover photos.
  • Safety first: the three checks, live space weather (it says NOT CHECKED if NASA's feed does not answer), a real-storm replay, a radiation line (about 25 microgray for this walk on a quiet day), an oxygen line (about 0.25 kg each: NASA's planning rate times the time outside) and a Mars daylight check.
  • Astronauts in pairs (EV1 and EV2), a route around obstacles, and three formats: a planner, a printed card and a screen for the walk.
  • Every number is tagged NASA data, derived or assumed, and a click opens its source.
  • What drives the checks, and what is context: the 1 m HiRISE height model sets every walking time and all three checks; Curiosity's storm readings drive the storm drill; NASA's live space-weather feed gives a clear or not-clear word. Shown for context only: the night heat layer, CTX, MOLA, the weather summaries and the rover photos.

How it is creative

  • One rule instead of separate ones: half speed, EV1 helping EV2, the reserve untouched, and 2 h of airlock time taken off first.
  • A leave-by time on the clock at every stop.
  • A breaking point for every check: how much slower the walk can get before it fails.
  • A check against the rover with a baseline: our error next to the error of a flat guess.

What we considered

  • Did we count all the time? Our first plan left out the time to get out and back in. NASA's study puts it at 2 h, so we added it. The third stop no longer fitted, so we made it optional and the app shows it failing.
  • Which check really decides? We expected the bad-day check. It is the suit-failure check, with 8 minutes to spare, and the app names it.
  • Whose numbers are these? Every rule is listed with its source. Two are our own choices and we say so: the 30 % reserve and the half speed.
  • How much oxygen? We wanted oxygen per metre. NASA's suited walking tests in Mars gravity started at 1.07 m/s, about twice our pace (EVA Walkback Test, NASA/TP-2009-214796), so an oxygen number per metre at our pace would be our own stretch. The app shows only NASA's hourly planning rate times the time outside, and says so.

Why it matters

  • A crew knows the last safe minute at every stop, and a bad plan fails at the planning table, not halfway through the walk.
  • The method needs only an elevation model and a few suit numbers, so it could be rebuilt for other Mars sites, for the Moon, or to tell hikers on Earth when to turn back.

Limits

Rocks under about 1.5 m are not in the elevation model. The walking curve was measured on hikers on Earth. The suit numbers are NASA's numbers for the Moon. Base camp is not a checked landing site. The Mars weather is from April 2024, not live. The Astronaut view follows the planned walk, not a real suit. These are planning assumptions for a hackathon prototype, not NASA flight rules.

Tools

Python (rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image), JavaScript, Leaflet and three.js, Node's test runner, GitHub Pages. The code is open source (Apache-2.0). Blender and FFmpeg made the video.

How we used AI

We used AI a lot, and we want to be exact about it.

What the AI did. An AI coding assistant (Claude, by Anthropic) wrote the code for the app, the data pipeline and the tests, directed by us. When we asked, it proposed the first version of the site, the four stops and the route rules. When we said the idea was not strong enough, it proposed "can the crew still get home?" as the main goal and the half-speed check. On the last day, AI agents read the 250 projects already submitted for this challenge and listed features worth adding. We approved the first six. For the others we let the AI choose and build, and it reported each one to us. Another AI agent then tested the new features on the live site, and its findings were fixed. The real-storm replay and the oxygen line came the same way: AI agents read NASA's radiation archive, its suit-test reports, its review of the Apollo moonwalk timelines and the RAD team's paper, and the AI re-checked their key numbers against the sources before using them. The oxygen line stayed a simple rate times time because NASA's Mars-gravity suit tests did not cover our pace. The AI also drafted the text of this page. In the video, the narration voice is AI-generated, and the astronaut figures in its 3D walk shots are the app's AI-generated 3D model; both are labelled on screen. No AI-generated video clip is in it. The spoken alerts in the app use the browser's own voice. The 3D walk page was also written by the AI assistant, and its astronaut figure is an AI-generated 3D model (Higgsfield), labelled on screen.

What we did. We picked the challenge. We decided which proposals to keep and which to drop. When the review showed that the airlock time was missing, we decided to count the full 2 h from NASA's Artemis III study and to take the third stop out of the default walk, even though it made our plan look smaller. We replaced the AI-made logo with one drawn from our own map.

What is not AI. All map, terrain, rover and weather data are real NASA, USGS and ESA data. The planner uses no AI image. The only AI-made picture in the app is the astronaut figure in the 3D walk, which is labelled on screen.
